rv.q: A virtually perfect big-budget, broad-appeal musical comedy that improves in every way over the 1992 film, director-choreographer Christopher Gattelli’s wildly entertaining vehicle for two of our best singer-actor-comedians on any stage today renders the movie-as-source snipe worthless.

That question pervades the 1992 film Death Becomes Her (written by Martin Donovan and David Koepp, and directed by Robert Zemeckis), which has just been turned into the funniest new musical comedy on Broadway.
Depending on your comic tastes, you're either on board for this ultimate vanity project or not.
Like its duelling antiheroines, Death Becomes Her refuses to die.
We would spend another hundred hours with these gals if given the chance, so why would they blink at eternity?
Whatever criticism gets hurled its way, nobody could reasonably say that “Death Becomes Her” looks cheap or lacks entertainment value.
Together they make musical-comedy magic—and musical comedy, when performed this well, never gets old.
Even if the musical doesn’t have a discernible heartbeat, Hilty and Simard ensure “Death Becomes Her” stays fun and fabulous.
The chance to see two theatrical masterminds go at it for a few hours is sufficient justification for the effort.
“Death Becomes Her” may be one of the funnier new musicals to splash down on Broadway, in a nearly blinding glare of sequins, in recent seasons.
With a crazed sense of humor and geysers of gore, these works demand recognition of simple and obvious facts: that looks aren’t everything and that everyone is going to die.
The conceit’s cleverly nipped and tucked, the work of fine theatrical plastic surgery, hard to dislike and ultimately—as a medical examiner might say of these women—without a heartbeat.
The relentless, deliciously played, perfectly directed hilarity of Death Becomes Her distinguishes this skillfully executed riot of a Broadway musical.
It's high camp and Broadway heaven, need I say more?
And it succeeds, spectacularly.
Thumbs up, three cheers, and a long, long, long life to Death Becomes Her.
Watching Hilty and Simard spar, singing the enjoyably apt score and chewing the scenery and each other is the musical event of the season so far.
Decadent and a lot of fun, Death Becomes Her is a musical that knows what it is and what its audience wants.
Death Becomes Her is intentional, which allows me to buy into the over the top comedy and violence and lack of limits.
The musical adaptation, newly arrived on Broadway after a Chicago tryout, is a laugh riot from start to finish, featuring superb comic performances from its two female leads.
It’s Tazewell’s costumes that seemed most fully to express the tone of the show: over-the-top but simultaneously making fun of how over-the-top it is — and having fun doing so.
Directing the new musical, Christopher Gattelli gleefully embraces the material’s inherent tackiness.
It's a mission that succeeds more often than not.
What “Death Becomes Her” lacks is even a remotely decent score.
Unfortunately, the Mattison-Carey score it boasts (?) resembles too many of the scores audiences presumably favor these days.
Death Becomes Her might be the best dark musical comedy to come along in decades.
I love this show! ... So hokey, funny, a take-off of old Hollywood musicals plus a bit of sci fi. I had a good time!
Death Becomes Her is a crowd-pleasing hit that deserves to be around forever — well, at least for a good long time.
The number, part of a Broadway show titled “Me Me Me,” is a showstopping kickoff to one of the funniest shows to hit the stage in years.

Megan Hilty has cemented a new “known for” role as a vain, two-time Oscar-nominated actress Madeline (the Streep character), eschewing traditional musical comic line readings with deliciously sassy lines “reads” worthy of RuPaul herself.
Death Becomes Her is nothing more and nothing less than the perfect guilty pleasure musical.
Look out world, Death Becomes Her: The Musical may just be the biggest body horror bitch-off on Broadway.

Naughty double entendres are sprinkled throughout, with mentions of cum guzzling, giving head, and fingering that aforementioned hole—you must believe me—and there’s also a fetching reference to Madeline having made it with her legs thrown wider than anyone, I mean higher than anyone....

cn.t: Critics largely embrace this campy musical adaptation as a hilarious crowd-pleaser that improves on the 1992 film, with standout performances from Megan Hilty and Jennifer Simard and dazzling production values delivering pure escapist fun.

vs.sum: A handsome Art Deco house with a distinctive celestial ceiling and wide auditorium. Sightlines are good from center seats but the wide layout means far-side seats lose some stage width. Notoriously narrow seats make comfort a challenge for longer shows.

acc.note: Step-free to lobby and Orchestra. Copper induction loop available. 5 wheelchair spaces.
